evals.prompt: Audit a product landing page where Lighthouse reports poor LCP and the hero is a 3200px JPEG from Sirv. Recommend and patch the image markup.
evals.expected_output: An evidence-first workflow that checks rendered markup/network data, removes lazy loading from the LCP image, adds explicit dimensions, responsive Sirv URLs, realistic sizes, preload/preconnect where appropriate, and verifies content type/size.
expectations: Inspects actual rendered HTML or build output before prescribing changes
Identifies the likely LCP image and does not lazy-load it
Uses explicit width/height or aspect-ratio to prevent CLS
Uses Sirv width candidates and realistic sizes instead of one oversized URL
Includes verification with audit-images, response headers, or Lighthouse/DevTools evidence

evals.prompt: A Next.js app uses product photos from a Sirv CDN. Add an image strategy that keeps Sirv transformations at the CDN and avoids double-compressing images.
evals.expected_output: A Next.js-aware solution that uses next/image with a custom Sirv loader or a justified alternative, sets width, quality, format=optimal, scale.option=noup, remotePatterns, realistic sizes, fetchPriority="high" instead of the Next.js 16-deprecated priority prop for the LCP image, and verifies the emitted URLs.
expectations: Chooses the framework-native image path before generic HTML snippets
Keeps Sirv as the transform layer when that is the intended CDN
Avoids double optimization or explains why layering is intentional
Sets realistic sizes and LCP priority (fetchPriority/preload, not the deprecated `priority` prop on Next.js 16+) only for above-fold images
Mentions verification of generated URLs and response content type

evals.prompt: Create a catalog image migration plan from local assets to Sirv, including metadata, searchability, and storefront delivery profiles.
evals.expected_output: A Sirv REST API plus Dynamic Imaging workflow: inventory assets, check limits, upload/fetch masters, preserve metadata/product fields, create reusable profiles, rewrite storefront URLs, and verify search, headers, and visual quality.
expectations: Uses Sirv REST API for inventory/upload/fetch/metadata
Preserves product metadata separately from HTML alt text
Uses profiles for repeated delivery recipes
Calls out path encoding, search pagination or scrolling, and token refresh
Includes a concrete verification plan

evals.prompt: Here is our product landing page HTML (evals/files/broken-landing.html). Find the image problems and fix the markup.
evals.expected_output: Runs the bundled audit script on the file, then fixes the lazy-loaded dimensionless hero, adds Sirv width candidates with realistic sizes, gives the grid images column-based sizes, adds alt and dimensions, right-sizes the 2400px logo, handles the CSS background, and reruns the audit to show fewer findings.
expectations: Runs audit-images.mjs on the fixture before editing
Removes loading="lazy" from the hero and adds fetchpriority="high" plus width/height
Replaces sizes="100vw" on the three-column grid images with a column-based value
Does not flag or rewrite the Cloudinary URLs as unoptimized
Fixes the oversized logo request (w=2400 in a 160px slot)
Reruns the audit after the fix and reports the difference

evals.prompt: Our Astro marketing site has a full-width hero set as a CSS background-image (a 2.4MB PNG photo in public/). LCP is 4.8s on mobile. Fix it.
evals.expected_output: Moves the hero to astro:assets (<Picture> or <Image>) from src/ with AVIF/WebP and width candidates, or keeps CSS with image-set() type() plus a responsive preload; marks it high priority and not lazy; reserves space; verifies LCP with Lighthouse or DevTools.
expectations: Explains that a CSS background in public/ is not discovered early and not optimized by Astro
Converts the photo from PNG to AVIF/WebP with responsive widths
Uses the framework-native Astro image path or image-set() with type(), not @supports url() checks
Makes the hero eager and high priority, with reserved layout space
Verifies LCP after the change

evals.prompt: We are on Next.js 16 with Cloudinary. Product cards use next/image with quality={85} and our hero uses priority. Images look soft and the hero is still slow. What is wrong?
evals.expected_output: Explains that Next.js 16 deprecates priority (use fetchPriority="high" or preload for one LCP image), that quality 85 is coerced to 75 unless images.qualities allows it, and that a Cloudinary loaderFile avoids double optimization; verifies emitted URLs and the LCP request.
expectations: Identifies that priority is deprecated in Next.js 16
Identifies the images.qualities default of [75] as the cause of soft images
Recommends a Cloudinary custom loader or explains the double-optimization trade-off
Verifies the emitted image URLs and LCP request priority

evals.prompt: Our homepage hero is a 40MB autoplaying MP4. Make it load faster.
evals.expected_output: Routes the video work to the video-optimization skill and handles only the image part (the poster frame as a likely LCP element).
expectations: Uses the video-optimization skill for encoding, streaming, and autoplay details
Does not treat the MP4 as an image format problem
Handles the poster image with image-optimization rules (size, format, priority)
